journal.hardwrought.first_edge.title: Something with an edge
journal.hardwrought.first_edge.text: My hands do nothing against rock or standing timber. I have to put an edge between them and me, and it has to be harder than both. There is a dark, glassy stone in the gravel and along the riverbeds that does not crumble — it splits, and where it splits it is sharper than anything else I have picked up. Tying one to a handle is the other half of the problem: leaves stripped off by hand give up a fibre that holds.
journal.hardwrought.bench_from_the_trunk: A bench out of the trunk

Two squares by two in my hands is not room enough for real work, and I have no way to saw a board. But a hatchet and a standing trunk might be. Felling it is not the point — the tree can stay where it is. Crouch against it, keep working the same spot, and do not stop after the first few strokes: it takes far more of them than it feels like it should.
journal.hardwrought.firmer_than_flint.te: Flint takes an edge and loses it again just as fast; a few good blows and the head is ruined. Now that I can break rock at all, the tougher material is in my own hands. A whole block of it is far too coarse to bind to a handle — but it comes apart into smaller pieces, and a head made of those lasts.
journal.hardwrought.heat_that_holds.text: An open fire cooks meat, and with a great deal of patience it will bake wet clay hard. That is as far as it goes; the heat goes straight up and is gone. What I need is something that keeps it in. The baked clay itself is the material for that — hard, all of a size, and it stacks. Enough of it, set into a closed square, and I have an oven instead of a fire pit.
journal.hardwrought.rust_in_the_rock.tex: Deep down there are rust-coloured streaks running through the stone, and a stone pick is only just enough to win them. What comes out is no use raw — soft, crumbling, half rock still. It wants to lie hot for a long time, longer than the clay did, and longer than an open fire has the patience for. What comes out of that holds an edge my stone hatchet is a toy beside.
journal.hardwrought.two_soft_metals.text: Copper on its own bends under the work; it is too soft for a tool. But there is a second metal, rarer, and it is not cut out of a seam at all — it is washed out of river gravel, a little at a time. Three parts of the first to one of the second is where I would start. Together they are not what either one is alone.
